name: REM sleep behaviour disorder
aliases: REM sleep without atonia with dream enactment

reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Results from loss of the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep, allowing patients to physically enact their dreams
Behaviours include talking, shouting, punching, kicking and leaping from bed, often mirroring vivid or violent dream content
Injuries to the patient or the bed partner are common and frequently prompt presentation
Episodes cluster in the latter half of the night when REM sleep predominates
Polysomnography confirming REM sleep without atonia is required for diagnosis
Idiopathic RBD is a strong prodromal marker of the synucleinopathies, notably Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy
Management combines clonazepam and/or melatonin with practical measures to make the sleeping environment safe
Secondary RBD can be provoked by antidepressants, other drugs, alcohol withdrawal or brainstem lesions
reference.pathophysiology: During normal REM sleep, brainstem circuits centred on the sublaterodorsal nucleus of the pons actively inhibit spinal motor neurones, producing the characteristic muscle atonia. In REM sleep behaviour disorder these circuits fail, so the motor accompaniments of dreaming are no longer suppressed and dreams are acted out. Because these pontine and medullary structures are affected early by alpha-synuclein pathology, the disorder often heralds a neurodegenerative synucleinopathy years before other features appear.
additionalDifferentials: Non-REM parasomnias such as sleepwalking, sleep terrors and confusional arousals
Obstructive sleep apnoea with arousals mimicking dream enactment (pseudo-RBD)
Nocturnal seizures, particularly of frontal lobe origin
additionalInvestigations: Video-polysomnography demonstrating REM sleep without atonia, with or without captured behaviours
Collateral history from the bed partner about the nature and timing of behaviours
Neurological examination for early parkinsonism or cognitive change
Review of medications, particularly antidepressants, and of alcohol use
MRI brain if a structural brainstem lesion is suspected, especially in younger patients
redFlags: Emerging parkinsonism, cognitive decline or autonomic failure suggesting evolving synucleinopathy
Onset in a young person or focal neurological signs pointing to a structural or demyelinating lesion
Serious injury to the patient or bed partner
Atypical features suggesting nocturnal seizures rather than a parasomnia
reference.prognosis: Symptoms are usually controllable with clonazepam or melatonin together with a safe sleep environment; however, most people with idiopathic RBD will develop a neurodegenerative synucleinopathy over subsequent years, so long-term neurological follow-up is advised.
pitfalls: Attributing dream enactment to nightmares without confirmatory polysomnography
Missing obstructive sleep apnoea causing pseudo-RBD
Neglecting bedroom safety advice, leaving the patient or partner at risk of injury
Failing to counsel appropriately and to monitor for later neurodegenerative disease
Overlooking an antidepressant or other drug as a precipitant
references: International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition (ICSD-3)
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (Kryger, Roth, Dement)
management: Make the sleep environment safe first, padding or lowering the bed, removing sharp objects and weapons, and considering separate sleeping arrangements for an injured bed partner
Melatonin as first-line pharmacotherapy to restore REM atonia with a favourable tolerability profile
Clonazepam where melatonin is insufficient, used with caution in older adults and those with cognitive impairment, gait instability or sleep apnoea
Review and withdraw precipitating drugs, especially serotonergic antidepressants, and reduce alcohol use
Identify and treat comorbid sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnoea, and assess for narcolepsy where suggested
Long-term neurological follow-up for emerging parkinsonism or cognitive change, as isolated disease is a strong prodrome of an alpha-synucleinopathy
Counsel the patient and family about injury prevention and the recognised risk of future neurodegenerative disease
